rules.title: Executable header inside a document file
rules.description: A Windows executable header was found inside a file whose name suggests a document or a picture. Documents and pictures do not normally carry an executable header.
rules.detail: The bytes at the start of the file match a Windows executable header, but the file name has a document or image extension.
rules.advice: Treat the file as an executable, whatever it is called. Do not open it. Ask the sender where it came from, and scan it with a full antivirus product.

rules.title: UPX packer marker
rules.description: The file contains the marker left by the UPX executable packer. Packed files are compressed on purpose, which makes them hard to read or review.
rules.detail: The UPX section marker was found in the file.
rules.advice: Packing is legitimate in some installers, so this is not proof of anything. If you did not expect a packed file, review it with a full antivirus product.

rules.title: Windows Script Host shell object
rules.description: The file mentions the Windows Script Host shell object, which is used to start other programs from a script.
rules.detail: A reference to the Windows Script Host shell object was found in the text.
rules.advice: Read the script and check what it starts. Administrative and installer scripts use this object as well.

rules.title: Antimalware scan interface bypass marker
rules.description: The file mentions the internal name of the antimalware scanning function. Legitimate software does not usually refer to it.
rules.detail: A reference to the antimalware scanning function was found in the text.
rules.advice: Review the file before running it. Software that refers to the antimalware scanning interface is worth a second look.

rules.title: PowerShell started with concealment switches
rules.description: The file starts PowerShell together with a switch that hides the window or bypasses the execution policy.
rules.detail: PowerShell was found together with a concealment switch on the same text.
rules.advice: Read the command line. Administrators use these switches for scheduled tasks, so context matters.

rules.title: Base64 decoding call
rules.description: The file decodes base64 data at runtime. That is a common way to hide the real content of a script.
rules.detail: A base64 decoding call was found in the text.
rules.advice: Decode the base64 text yourself and read it before running the script. Many tools do this, so this is a hint and not a verdict.

rules.title: Command that deletes volume shadow copies
rules.description: The file contains a command that deletes volume shadow copies or turns off recovery. Administrators use these commands when they clear disk space, so the context decides what it means.
rules.detail: A command that deletes volume shadow copies or switches recovery off was found in the text.
rules.advice: Find out who wrote the script and why it needs the recovery points removed. Without them the machine has no way back to the files it held before.

patterns.value: vssadmin delete shadows,wmic shadowcopy delete,wbadmin delete,resize shadowstorage,recoveryenabled no,delete shadows /all,shadowcopy delete

rules.title: Wording used in a ransom note
rules.description: The text says that files have been encrypted and asks for payment. The wording on its own is not proof of anything, but this shape does not turn up in ordinary documents.
rules.detail: The text carries the wording of a note that announces encrypted files and asks for payment.
rules.advice: Do not pay anything yet. Keep a copy of the note, and have the file looked at in a safe place before you do anything else with it.

patterns.value: your files have been encrypted,all your files are encrypted,your files are encrypted,files have been encrypted,all files have been encrypted|decrypt,decryption key,bitcoin,ransom,payment,restore your files,recover your files
